Understanding Tax Sales in Duval County, Texas

Duval County, Texas, conducts tax sales to recover unpaid property taxes. These sales provide opportunities for investors while ensuring the county collects revenue to fund public services. Here’s a concise overview of how these auctions are handled and what you need to know if you’re planning to participate.

1. Notification and Advertising

Before the auction, the county notifies delinquent property owners about the overdue taxes and the sale. Properties listed for auction are advertised in a local newspaper for three consecutive weeks. These advertisements include essential details such as the sale’s date, time, location, and property descriptions.

The county may also provide this information online, offering easy access to prospective bidders. Check out our Auction Calendar for scheduled auctions.

2. Registration Process

To bid at a tax sale, you must register with the county’s designated official. This involves presenting a valid form of identification and completing any required forms. Registration is typically available in the days leading up to the auction and may also be offered on the day of the event. Ensure the name you register under is accurate, as it will appear on the deed if you’re the successful bidder.

3. The Auction

Tax sales in Duval County are public auctions, often conducted orally. Properties are sold to the highest bidder, with opening bids typically covering the taxes owed, interest, penalties, and related costs. Payment is required immediately and must be made using cash or a cashier’s check. Personal checks are not accepted. The county official conducting the sale will outline the bidding rules before the auction begins, so it’s important to arrive early and listen carefully.

4. Deed and Ownership

Winning bidders receive a Sheriff’s Deed. However, the deed comes without warranties or guarantees, which means you’re responsible for understanding the property’s condition and any associated risks. Title insurance may not be available. It’s also worth noting that the Sheriff’s Deed does not extinguish certain liens, such as IRS liens, so thorough research is critical.

5. Redemption Period

Texas law allows former property owners a redemption period to reclaim their property. For homestead and agricultural properties, this period is two years. For other properties, it’s 180 days. To redeem, owners must pay the purchase price, recording fees, taxes paid by the buyer, and an additional redemption premium. This premium is 25% of the purchase price if redeemed within the first year and 50% if redeemed during the second year for applicable properties.

6. Research and Responsibilities

As a buyer, you’re responsible for any taxes accrued after the sale date. It’s essential to conduct thorough research on the property beforehand. This includes checking for existing liens or encumbrances, verifying zoning restrictions, and assessing the property’s physical condition. Consider visiting the property in person and consulting with a real estate professional to evaluate its potential value and risks.

7. Post-Sale Steps

After purchasing a property at a tax sale, you must record the deed with the county clerk’s office. This step is crucial to establish your ownership. Additionally, it’s recommended to consult with an attorney or title company to address any outstanding legal or title issues.
